catalog_quote: En el mixteco del norte de Tlaxiaco, las palabras básicas se componen de dos sílabas. La sílaba tónica o acentuada se pronuncia con más fuerza y siempre es la penúltima sílaba (antes de la última). [p. 6] ... Las vocales cortadas por el saltillo aparecen solamente en la sílaba tónica de la palabra, es decir, en la sílaba que tiene mayor prominencia. En español la acentuación no es completamente regular y por eso, algunas veces es necesario marcar la sílaba tónica con un signo de acento (tilde) sobre las vocales (á, é, í, ó, ú). Sin embargo, en mixteco, la acentuación es regular y predecible; el acento siempre recae sobre la penúltima sílaba de la palabra. La sílaba tónica aparece subrayada en los siguientes ejemplos: yuu petate / veꞌe casa / ndiaꞌa ver / iaa agrio [pp. 7-8] ||| Gittlen & Marlett 1985: 176-177: Compounds and loanwords account for all nouns of more than two syllables. Compounding and affixation, discussed below, account for verb forms which are more than two syllables in length. ... Primary word stress always falls on the penultimate syllable of the word in NM. In the following formalization of this generalization, X0 is understood to vary over all word-level syntactic category labels. (5) Stress Assignment: V ---> [+ stress] / ___ (C0)V]X0

new_statements.translation: In Northern Tlaxiaco Mixtec, basic words consist of two syllables. The tonic or stressed syllable is pronounced with more force and is always the penultimate syllable (the one before the last). ... Vowels cut by the glottal stop appear only in the tonic syllable of the word, i.e. the syllable with greatest prominence. In Spanish accentuation is not completely regular ... However, in Mixtec, accentuation is regular and predictable; the stress always falls on the penultimate syllable of the word.

En españo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the word (basic roots are disyllabic couplets, so stress = couplet-initial); glottalized/checked vowels are licensed only in the stressed syllable. Corroborated by Gittlen & Marlett 1985:176-177 'Primary word stress always falls on the penultimate syllable of the word in NM' with rule V -> [+stress] / __ (C0)V]word.
new_statements.exceptions: Reduced (truncated) first members of compounds lose their stress, the compound keeps penultimate stress (2016 p.8; 1985 p.188); in plural forms of directional motion verbs stress no longer falls on the root's tonic syllable but on the plural suffix -kuei, which itself has the penultimate pattern of a normal word (2016 p.15; 1985 p.189); monosyllabic dependent words/clitics do not stand alone. Language is also tonal (three levels: high, mid, low), tone unmarked in the practical orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (phonological) word including suffix -kuei and compounds; enclitic pronouns written as separate words. Description based on San Juan Ñumí speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe the speech of San Juan Ñumí ('Ñumí Mixtec', NM), the reference variety for ISO xtn / Glottolog nort2985 Northern Tlaxiaco Mixtec; the SIL page notes the code also covers Santiago Nundiche, San Sebastián Nicananduta and San Antonino Monteverde with 'clear differences among them'.

new_statements.quote: [p.6] También una palabra puede tener una sílaba tónica, o sea, una sílaba que pronunciamos con más fuerza. En mixteco la sílaba más fuerte siempre es la penúltima. Lea las siguientes palabras en voz alta, pensando en las sílabas tónicas. [p.39] Las dos vocales se consideran dos sílabas, como te.e (escribir). Así se conserva el patrón del acento, o vocal más fuerte, en la penúltima sílaba de las palabras independientes del mixteco. [p.83] Ya se ha mencionado que la vocal cortada se presenta solamente en la sílaba tónica de palabras. Hay una sola sílaba tónica, entonces no es posible escribir dos saltillos en una sola palabra.
new_statements.translation: [p.6] A word can also have a tonic syllable, that is, a syllable that we pronounce with more force. In Mixtec the strongest syllable is always the penultimate. Read the following words aloud, thinking about the tonic syllables. [p.39] The two vowels are counted as two syllables, as in te.e 'to write'. In this way the stress pattern, i.e. the strongest vowel, is kept on the penultimate syllable of independent Mixtec words. [p.83] It has already been mentioned that the checked (glottalized) vowel occurs only in the tonic syllable of words. There is only one tonic syllable, so it is not possible to write two saltillos in a single word.
new_statements.citation: Gittlen, Peter and Laura Gittlen. 2008. Cómo escribimos en el mixteco del norte de Tlaxiaco, Volumen 1: Sonidos y letras. México: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. 125 pp.

Title page (p.1-2): 'Cómo escribimos en el mixteco del norte de Tlaxiaco, Volumen 1: Sonidos y letras. Pedro Gittlen, Laura Gittlen. Printed p.6 = p.9 (footer 'Lección 1: Repaso de las letras iguales al español 6'): 'También una palabra puede tener una sílaba tónica, o sea, una sílaba que pronunciamos con más fuerza. En mixteco la sílaba más fuerte siempre es la penúltima. Lea las siguientes palabras en voz alta, pensando en las sílabas tónicas.' followed by examples lamu, chitu, inu, kasa,…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate, penultimate stress) and the Gittlen 2016 statement; adds that vowel length counts as two syllables for the count, that there is a single stressed syllable per word, and that glottalized vowels are confined to it. Note the listed open_url (mexico.sil.org search page) was blocked by an automated-access block on both attempts; the book was obtained from the the Internet Archive capture (20120710234929) of the old SIL Mexico PDF, which is the 2008 2nd (electronic) edition of this same title (title page: Pedro Gittlen, Laura Gittlen, Segunda edición 2008).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (the 'strongest' syllable) always falls on the penultimate syllable of an independent word; a long/double vowel counts as two syllables (te.e), so a CVV word is stressed on its first vowel; exactly one stressed syllable per word; the checked vowel (saltillo) can only occur in that penultimate stressed syllable. Tone is contrastive (p.59 'in' one vs 'iin' nine; p.117 yaku/yaku) but is not written and is not said to affect stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned (explicitly one tonic syllable per word, p.83)
new_statements.exceptions: none for stress placement; note the syllabification convention that double vowels are two syllables and the last vowel of a VV sequence is the final syllable (p.39); Spanish loans keep Spanish accents in spelling (p.109)
new_statements.identity_note: Gittlen & Marlett 1985 describes 'Ñumí Mixtec', the speech of San Juan Ñumí and San Antonio Nduaxico in the district of Tlaxiaco (footnote *, p.192), which falls under ISO xtn / Glottolog nort2985 Northern Tlaxiaco Mixtec; the 2008 orthography book is written for xtn as a whole and notes lexical variation between towns (p.117) while treating it as one language.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees on penultimate placement; adds the formal rule, the compound-word domain (one penultimate stress per compound after truncation), the ordering of stress assignment relative to the segmental rules, and the restriction of checked vowels to the stressed syllable. The paper's 'Ñumí Mixtec' is the variety of San Juan Ñumí / San Antonio Nduaxico, district of Tlaxiaco (footnote *, p.192), which is within the ISO xtn Northern Tlaxiaco Mixtec grouping.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is assigned to the vowel followed by exactly one more syllable before the word-level bracket, i.e. the penultimate syllable of every word regardless of category. In compounds the first member is truncated and loses its stress; the compound as a whole carries a single penultimate stress. Glottalized (checked) vowels and complex onsets occur only in the stressed syllable. Tone exists (the prefix /xi-/ carries a high tone) but 'the analysis of tone is incomplete' (p.185).
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned; only 'primary word stress' is defined and compounds are said to keep a single penultimate stress
new_statements.exceptions: none for placement; Stress Assignment is ordered after Vocalization and Vowel Epenthesis and before /xi/-Deletion etc. in the rule chain (30), p.186; the plural word kwei with motion verbs is stressed like an ordinary word (p.189)
new_statements.identity_note: Gittlen & Marlett 1985 describes 'Ñumí Mixtec', the speech of San Juan Ñumí and San Antonio Nduaxico in the district of Tlaxiaco (footnote *, p.192), which falls under ISO xtn / Glottolog nort2985 Northern Tlaxiaco Mixtec; the 2008 orthography book is written for xtn as a whole and notes lexical variation between towns (p.117) while treating it as one language.
